lessons.title: Celebrating difference: respect for everyone
objectives: Explain that people are different and equally valuable
Challenge stereotypes with examples
Show respect in words and actions

keywords.def: the variety of people and cultures in the world
an unfair fixed idea about a group of people
treating others with care and dignity
having the same value and rights
an unfair opinion formed without knowing the facts

starter: Name one way to be kind to a classmate.
Why should we avoid unkind nicknames?

teach.heading: We are all different
bullets: All are made by Allah and valuable
teach.note: Say bismillah. Ask pupils to share (right to pass) something that makes them unique, e.g. a language they speak, a food they like, a hobby. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day. Emphasise that we celebrate difference while holding to our values. Misconception: ‘different’ means ‘worse’. It does not.

teach.heading: A message from the Qur'an
bullets: Qur'an 49:13: people made into nations and tribes
So that we may know one another
The best of us is the most God-conscious
teach.note: Cite plainly Qur'an 49:13: Allah made humanity into peoples and tribes so that they may know one another, and the most honoured is the one with the most taqwa. Ask: ‘What does this teach about how we treat others?’ Take answers. Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass values of Integrity and Eeman.

teach.heading: Stereotypes
bullets: A stereotype is a fixed idea about a group
‘All boys like football’ is a stereotype
teach.note: Ask pupils to think of a stereotype, such as ‘girls cannot be engineers’ or ‘old people cannot use technology’. Challenge each with a counter-example. Model how a stereotype can hurt. Remind pupils to use invented examples, not real classmates. Check understanding with thumbs up or down.

teach.heading: Showing respect
bullets: Do not make fun of differences
teach.note: Role-play a scenario where one pupil makes a comment about another's lunch or accent. Ask the class to suggest respectful responses. Connect to adab and the Equality Act: schools must protect people from unfair treatment because of characteristics such as race, religion, disability, sex and age. Keep wording simple.

practice: Sort into respectful or disrespectful: (a) listening to someone's idea (b) laughing at an accent (c) asking about their favourite food (d) copying someone's mistake to tease.
Challenge this stereotype: ‘Only adults can make a difference.’ Write a counter-example.
What could you say if someone mocks another person's lunch?
independent: Create a ‘We are all different’ poster with five ways people differ and one sentence about respect.
Write what Qur'an 49:13 teaches in your own words.
Role-play: respond kindly to an unkind comment.
exit: Define stereotype in your own words.
Give one way to show respect to someone different from you.
lessons.homework: Interview a family member about a time they felt included or excluded and write three sentences about what you learned.
lessons.send: SEND: use symbol cards and sentence starters. EAL: key vocabulary with images. Stretch: research a famous person who challenged a stereotype.

lessons.title: Bullying and cyberbullying: spotting it and stopping it
objectives: Describe different kinds of bullying, including online
Know how to respond and who to tell
Explain how to be an upstander safely

keywords.def: hurting someone on purpose, again and again
bullying that happens online or by phone
someone who sees bullying but does nothing
someone who supports a person being bullied
to tell a trusted adult or the platform

starter: Name two ways to be respectful.
Give one reason why people are valuable.

teach.heading: Kinds of bullying
teach.note: Say bismillah. Recap the difference between falling out and bullying from Year 3. Add that bullying can be hidden, such as exclusion. Ask: ‘Can bullying happen without anyone touching someone?’ Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day. Use invented scenarios only.

teach.heading: Why online is different
bullets: Messages can be seen by many
It can happen at any time
People may hide behind a screen
Words and images can stay online
teach.note: Explain that cyberbullying can follow someone home, since messages may arrive late at night. People may say things online they would not say face to face. Ask: ‘What can we do before pressing send?’ Teach the THINK check: is it True, Helpful, Inspiring, Necessary, Kind?

teach.heading: How it feels
bullets: Afraid to go to school or log in
teach.note: Be sensitive and supportive. Link to Islamic teaching: Qur'an 49:11 forbids mocking others. Remind pupils that the Prophet (peace be upon him) said a Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand people are safe (Bukhari and Muslim). Ask pupils to give advice to a friend who is being bullied.

teach.heading: What to do
bullets: Tell a trusted adult and keep telling
teach.note: Teach the response chain: Stop, Save, Block, Tell. Stress that adults want to hear and will help. Explain how to be an upstander safely: do not join in, support the person, report. Remind them of Childline (0800 1111) as a free confidential helpline.

practice: Is this cyberbullying? (a) A group chat where everyone mocks one child. (b) A friend disagrees politely about a game. (c) Someone shares an embarrassing photo without asking.
Use the THINK check on this message: ‘Nobody likes you, just leave.’
Write two sentences of advice to a child who is being bullied online.
independent: Create a ‘Stop, Save, Block, Tell’ guide with one sentence per step.
Write a script for an upstander message to support a friend who was left out of a group chat.
List three trusted adults and one helpline you could contact.
exit: Name two differences between face-to-face bullying and cyberbullying.
What are the four steps if you receive bullying messages?
lessons.homework: Make a family agreement on kind online behaviour and ask a parent or carer to sign it.
lessons.send: SEND: provide visual steps and scripts. EAL: pre-teach ‘retaliate’, ‘evidence’, ‘report’. Stretch: write advice for a school newsletter on being an upstander.

lessons.title: Feelings and worries: understanding and managing them
objectives: Name a range of feelings and where we feel them
Describe strategies for managing worry or anger
Link patience (sabr) and remembrance of Allah to wellbeing

keywords.def: a feeling such as happy, sad, angry or worried
a feeling of being anxious about something
peaceful and relaxed
patience and steadfastness
a plan or method that helps

starter: Name two ways to be a good upstander.
What are the four steps for cyberbullying?

teach.heading: Feelings are normal
bullets: All feelings are part of being human
Feelings can be big or small
It is okay to ask for help
teach.note: Say bismillah. Show an emotion wheel. Ask pupils to pick one word that matches how they feel (private choice). Normalise: even the Prophets experienced sadness; do not give details unless sure. Keep to: feelings are part of being human and we respond with good character. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day.

teach.heading: Where do we feel it?
bullets: Notice the clues in your body
teach.note: Use a body outline. Pupils name signs of each feeling in the chat. This helps them notice feelings early. Misconception: ‘If I’m worried, something is wrong with me.’ Everyone worries.

teach.heading: Ways to feel calmer
bullets: Slow breathing: in for 4, out for 6
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 13:28 says that hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah. Practise a calm breathing exercise for one minute. Introduce the ‘worry box’ idea: write a worry and share it with a trusted adult. Encourage dua and dhikr alongside practical strategies and talking to others.

teach.heading: Patience and hope
bullets: Hard times do not last forever
Seek help from family and teachers
teach.note: Cite plainly: Qur'an 94:5-6, ‘with hardship comes ease’. Ask: ‘How did you cope the last time something felt difficult?’ Take volunteers. Link to the Tarbiyyah Compass value of Resilience. Reassure pupils that asking for help is a strength. If a pupil appears very distressed, speak to the DSL.

practice: Match feeling to body clue: worried / angry / sad / excited → hot face / tight tummy / heavy chest / bouncy legs.
Try the breathing: in for 4, out for 6, three times. How do you feel?
Choose two strategies for when you feel angry. Why will they help?
independent: Make a ‘calm toolbox’ with five strategies that work for you.
Write a message to a friend who is worried about a test, using two strategies.
Draw or write about a time you felt proud after getting through something difficult.
exit: Name two ways to help yourself feel calm.
What does Qur'an 94:5-6 teach about difficulty?
lessons.homework: Practise one calming strategy each day this week and write a sentence about how it felt.
lessons.send: SEND: provide an emotion chart and picture strategies. EAL: translate feelings vocabulary and use gestures. Stretch: create a short guide for younger pupils on dealing with worry.

lessons.title: Privacy, secrets and asking for help
objectives: Tell the difference between safe surprises and unsafe secrets
Explain that our bodies and personal space are private
Name people and services who can help

keywords.def: the right to keep some things to yourself
something kept secret for a short time that makes people happy
something you are asked not to tell
a limit that protects you or others
a service you can contact for advice and support

starter: Name one way to feel calm.

teach.heading: Our bodies are private
bullets: Private parts are covered by underwear
Nobody should touch them or ask to see them
teach.note: Say bismillah. Use the NSPCC ‘PANTS’ rule as a framework: Privates are private; Always remember your body belongs to you; No means no; Talk about secrets that upset you; Speak up, someone can help. Use correct, simple language and keep a calm tone. Recap Year 1 ‘My body belongs to me’. Ground rules: right to pass, no personal stories, kindness. Anonymous questions can go to the teacher's question box. If a pupil says anything that worries you, stay calm, do not promise secrecy and follow the Child Protection and Safeguarding Policy: tell the DSL the same day. Remind that Islam teaches modesty and respect for privacy; adults must also respect children's privacy and safety.

teach.heading: Surprises or secrets?
bullets: Surprise: a happy secret, told soon
Unsafe secret: makes you worried or scared
Never keep a secret that hurts you
teach.note: Give invented examples: a surprise gift for Eid (safe) versus someone saying, ‘Don’t tell anyone what happened.’ Ask pupils to give a thumbs up or down for safe or unsafe. Emphasise: if a secret makes you feel worried, tell. You will never be in trouble for telling.

teach.heading: Online privacy
bullets: Only talk to people you know
Tell an adult about pressure to send things
Adults must never ask for secrets
teach.note: Link to Year 3 online safety. Explain that anyone who asks you to keep online chats secret from your family should be reported. Teach the ‘trusted network’: five people or places to go to. Ask: ‘Who is on your hand?’ Draw a hand and write a trusted adult on each finger.

teach.heading: Getting help
bullets: Tell a trusted adult at school or home
teach.note: Share the helpline numbers and website in the follow-up message to parents. Practise a short script: ‘I need to tell you something that is worrying me.’ Reassure pupils. If any pupil discloses harm or fear, follow safeguarding procedures: listen, do not promise secrecy, tell the DSL the same day.

practice: Safe surprise or unsafe secret? (a) A surprise meal you are making for your grandmother. (b) An adult asking you to hide a message from your parents. (c) A gift you hide until Eid. (d) A friend makes you promise not to tell about being hurt.
Draw your hand and name five people you could tell.
Practise saying ‘No, I don’t like that’ in a calm, firm voice.
independent: Write a short script of how you would tell a trusted adult about a worry.
Make a poster ‘Speak up, someone can help’ with the Childline number.
Write three sentences explaining the difference between a surprise and an unsafe secret.
exit: Give one example of a safe surprise and one of an unsafe secret.
Name two people or services you could tell.
lessons.homework: Tell a trusted adult at home what you learned about private parts and safe secrets, and agree on a family ‘safe word’ if they wish.
lessons.send: SEND: use picture sorting cards and a script card. EAL: use the PANTS visuals with simple key words. Stretch: write a letter to a younger child about speaking up.

lessons.title: Keeping track of my money
lessons.bigQuestion: Your money box had £5 last month and has £2 now. How could you find out where the £3 went?
objectives: To understand how keeping a record of money in and out helps us make good choices
successCriteria: All: say what money in and money out mean
Most: complete a simple money record and find the balance
Some: explain how a record helps us save for a goal
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty and responsibility with money

keywords.def: money that comes in
money that goes out
the money left after spending
a written list to keep track

hook.text: Your money box had £5 last month and has £2 now. How could you find out where the £3 went?
hook.a: Keep a record of every amount in and out.

islamicLink.text: Allah commands writing down debts and agreements (al-Baqarah 2:282, the longest ayah of the Qur'an). Keeping clear records of money is part of honesty and good management.

starter.q: Is a coat a need or a want?
Name a safe place to keep money at home.
starter.a: A money box (kept by a grown-up).

teach.heading: Money in, money out
bullets: Out: things we buy, sadaqah we give
teach.note: Use simple amounts.

teach.heading: A money record
teach.note: Model.

teach.heading: Model: finding the balance
teach.note: Model.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

practice.q: Balance £2.00. Pocket money £3.00 comes in. New balance?
Balance £5.00. Buy a book for £3.50. New balance?
Why record sadaqah as money out?
practice.a: Because it leaves our money box; we still count it so the balance is right.

independent.q: Core: Complete the money record sheet (6 lines) and find the final balance (pupil PDF).
independent.a: Final balance on the teacher key: £4.30.

independent.q: Extend: How many weeks of £1.50 savings to reach £9?
independent.a: 6 weeks

independent.q: Stretch: Explain how a record helps you save for something you want.
independent.a: You can see where money goes, cut wants and watch the balance grow.

exit.q: The money left after spending is the... A) income B) balance C) price
exit.a: B) balance

exit.q: Big question: how could you find where £3 went?
exit.a: Keep a record of money in and out.

lessons.homework: Start a money record for one week with a grown-up (real or pretend pocket money).
lessons.send: SEND: coins to count and a record with in/out columns only. EAL: income, spending, balance. Stretch: add a 'savings goal' column.

lessons.title: Paying for goods
lessons.bigQuestion: When a grown-up taps a card, money disappears without coins. How do they know how much they spent?
objectives: To understand the different ways people pay for things and how to check change
successCriteria: All: name three ways to pay (cash, card, phone)
Most: work out change from a purchase
Some: explain why card payments still need careful checking
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty in buying and selling

keywords.def: coins and notes
a card that takes money straight from a bank account
money given back when you pay too much
a paper or digital record of what was bought

hook.text: When a grown-up taps a card, money disappears without coins. How do they know how much they spent?
hook.a: They check the receipt and their bank account.

islamicLink.text: Islam teaches fair trade: the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever cheats is not one of us (Muslim). Paying the right price and checking change honestly are part of good character.

teach.heading: Ways to pay
bullets: Debit card: from a bank account
Phone or online: still from an account
teach.note: Children use cash; adults may use cards. Never use a grown-up's card without permission.

teach.heading: Working out change
teach.note: Model.

model.problem: A sandwich costs £2.35. You pay with £5. Change?

teach.heading: Receipts
bullets: Show what was bought and the price
teach.note: Show a supermarket receipt (no personal details).

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: You pay £1 for an 85p drink. Change?

practice.q: Price £3.60, paid £5. Change?
practice.model: Teacher counts up: 40p to £4, then £1 to £5: £1.40.

practice.q: Price £7.25, paid £10. Change?

independent.q: Core: Shop role-play sheet: find the change for six purchases (pupil PDF).
independent.a: Answers on the teacher key.

independent.q: Extend: A receipt says £4.50 but the shelf said £3.50. What should you do?
independent.a: Politely ask the shop to check: you may have been overcharged £1.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why paying by card can make it easier to overspend.
independent.a: You do not see money leave, so it is easy to lose track.

exit.q: A receipt is... A) a type of coin B) a record of what was bought C) a bank
exit.a: B) a record of what was bought
options: A record of what was bought

exit.q: Big question: how does a grown-up know what a card payment cost?
exit.a: The receipt and the bank account.

lessons.homework: Look at a shopping receipt with a grown-up and find the most and least expensive items.
lessons.send: SEND: coins to count up. EAL: change, receipt, price. Stretch: find change from £20.

lessons.title: Family expenses
lessons.bigQuestion: What does it cost to switch on a light at home? Who pays?
objectives: To understand what a family spends money on and why needs come first
successCriteria: All: name four family expenses
Most: sort expenses into needs and wants
Some: explain why bills must be paid before treats
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: adding money and comparing totals
lessons.smsc: Moral: gratitude to parents and not wasting

keywords.def: something money is spent on
a request to pay for a service, like electricity
something a family must pay for
a plan for spending money

hook.text: What does it cost to switch on a light at home? Who pays?
hook.a: Electricity costs money; grown-ups pay a bill for it.

islamicLink.text: Islam asks parents to provide for their families, and asks children to thank and respect their parents. Allah says: 'And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy' (al-Isra 17:24).

starter.a: A record of what was bought.

teach.heading: What families pay for
teach.note: Do not ask pupils how much their family earns or spends.

teach.heading: Needs before wants
teach.note: Sort.

teach.heading: Saving energy saves money
bullets: Lights off when leaving a room
teach.note: We can help the family budget.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.why: Water is needed for life and hygiene; the others are wants.

practice.q: Why is internet essential for our family at TGA?
practice.a: Our lessons are online on Teams.
practice.model: Teacher links: our school is online, so internet is a need for learning.

practice.q: Name two ways you can save energy at home.
practice.a: Lights off, shorter showers, close the fridge.

independent.q: Core: Pretend family budget: £100 for the week. Choose spending from the price list so essentials come first (pupil PDF).
independent.a: Essentials (food, bills) chosen first and total no more than £100.

independent.q: Extend: Write a thank-you note to a grown-up for something they pay for.
independent.a: A short thank-you note.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why bills must be paid before treats.
independent.a: Without paying bills, the family could lose essentials like electricity or water.

exit.q: A bill is... A) a toy B) a request to pay for a service C) a coin
exit.a: B) a request to pay for a service
options: A request to pay for a service

exit.q: Big question: who pays for the light at home, and how?
exit.a: Grown-ups, by paying the electricity bill.

lessons.homework: Do one energy-saving job at home every day this week.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards of expenses. EAL: bill, expense, essential. Stretch: work out how much is left from £100.

lessons.title: Planning and budgeting
lessons.bigQuestion: You get £10 for Eid. Would you spend it all at once, save it, or share some? Why?
objectives: To understand how a budget helps us plan spending, saving and giving
successCriteria: All: say what a budget is
Most: split an amount into spend, save and give
Some: adjust a budget when something changes
lessons.smsc: Moral: balance between spending, saving and giving

keywords.def: a plan for how to use money
keep money for later
share money with people in need
something we plan and work towards

hook.text: You get £10 for Eid. Would you spend it all at once, save it, or share some? Why?

islamicLink.text: Allah praises those who 'when they spend, are neither wasteful nor stingy, but in between' (al-Furqan 25:67). A budget helps us find that middle way.

starter.q: Which is essential? A) water bill B) cinema
Name a way to save energy.

teach.heading: What is a budget?
teach.note: A budget stops money running out.

teach.heading: Spend, save, give
teach.note: Model splitting £10.

teach.heading: Model: making a budget
teach.note: Model.

steps: Spend: £5 on a snack and stationery

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.q: Budget £10: give £1, save £4. How much to spend?

practice.q: Budget £20: give £2, save £8. Spend?
A £15 book: saving £3 a week, how many weeks?

independent.q: Core: Make your own budget for £10 of Eid money with spend, save and give amounts that add up (pupil PDF).
independent.a: Three amounts adding to £10 with reasons.

independent.q: Extend: Your goal costs £12 and you save £2 a week. When will you reach it?
independent.a: After 6 weeks.

independent.q: Stretch: A friend's birthday gift costs £3 this week. Change your budget and explain.
independent.a: Take £3 from spending (not giving) so savings stay on track.

exit.q: A budget is... A) a bill B) a plan for using money C) a coin
exit.a: B) a plan for using money

exit.q: Big question: what would you do with £10, and why?
exit.a: For example: give £1, save £4, spend £5, to keep a balance.

lessons.homework: Make a budget for any money you receive this month with a grown-up.
lessons.send: SEND: three labelled pots with coins. EAL: spend, save, give. Stretch: plan a budget over 4 weeks.

lessons.title: Charity work: sadaqah and zakah
lessons.bigQuestion: Can you give sadaqah if you have no money at all?
objectives: To understand how sadaqah and zakah help people in need and how they differ
successCriteria: All: say what sadaqah is
Most: explain how zakah is different from sadaqah
Some: plan a sadaqah action at home (no collecting from the public)
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: percentages (2.5%) for older pupils; RE: the five pillars
lessons.smsc: Spiritual and moral: generosity and caring for the needy

keywords.def: voluntary giving to help others (صَدَقَة)
the obligatory yearly charity on savings (زَكَاة)
helping people in need
the minimum wealth before zakah is due (نِصَاب)

hook.text: Can you give sadaqah if you have no money at all?
hook.a: Yes: a smile, a kind word or helping someone are all sadaqah.

islamicLink.text: Zakah is one of the five pillars of Islam. The Prophet ﷺ taught that every good deed is sadaqah (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and that the upper hand (the giver) is better than the lower hand (al-Bukhari and Muslim).

starter.a: Something we must have to live.

teach.heading: Sadaqah
teach.note: Examples: a smile, removing something harmful from a path, helping at home.

teach.heading: Zakah
bullets: 2.5% of savings kept for a year above the nisab
Given to set groups of people (at-Tawbah 9:60)
teach.note: Children do not usually pay zakah themselves; families do.

teach.heading: Giving safely
bullets: Through trusted charities or the masjid
No collecting money from the public
teach.note: School rule: sadaqah plans are at home with family.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Launch the poll.

check.why: Zakah is a pillar; sadaqah is voluntary (and always encouraged).

practice.q: Name three kinds of sadaqah that cost no money.
practice.a: A smile, helping someone, kind words.
practice.model: Teacher names a smile and helping a neighbour carry shopping.

practice.q: A family has £1000 savings kept for a year, above the nisab. Zakah at 2.5%?

independent.q: Core: Plan a 'sadaqah week' at home: one kind act or gift each day (pupil PDF).
independent.a: Seven sadaqah actions planned with a grown-up.
independent.model: Teacher plans Monday: help prepare dinner.

independent.q: Extend: Write how sadaqah and zakah are different in two sentences.
independent.a: Sadaqah is voluntary and any amount; zakah is obligatory, 2.5% of savings above nisab each year.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain why Islam makes zakah obligatory, not just optional.
independent.a: So the needy are always helped and wealth is shared fairly.

exit.q: Zakah is... A) 2.5% of savings above nisab B) 50% of all money C) only a smile
exit.a: A) 2.5% of savings above nisab

exit.q: Big question: can you give sadaqah with no money?
exit.a: Yes: kind acts like a smile or helping are sadaqah.

lessons.homework: Carry out your sadaqah week with your family and tick each day.
lessons.send: SEND: picture cards of sadaqah acts. EAL: sadaqah, zakah, charity. Stretch: find out the eight groups who receive zakah (at-Tawbah 9:60).

lessons.title: The real cost of chocolate
lessons.bigQuestion: A chocolate bar costs about £1. Who do you think gets most of that pound: the farmer, the factory or the shop?
objectives: To understand that the price of a product hides the work of many people, and that farmers are often paid very little
successCriteria: All: list three stages in making chocolate
Most: explain who gets the most money from a bar
Some: explain why a low price for us can mean low pay for farmers
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: sharing £1 into parts (fractions and money)

keywords.def: all the steps from grower to shop
a person who grows crops
